Opening

BUILD · SCIENCE · W13A · 2 MINUTES

Fair Test Planner: Change One Thing

Learning objective

I can plan a controlled water-passage comparison and a separate method pilot.

Success looks like

  • Name the change and measure with a unit.
  • Specify at least three important controls.
  • Plan repeats, a pilot and a safety stop without inventing results.

A fair comparison begins before the numbers. Build the method, not a result that looks tidy.

W13A · one 40-minute lesson

Seven stages, with one arrival and one exit. Use the route that helps you show your science today.

No earlier worksheet is needed. Fresh evidence is included.

Point, speak, sign, move cards, draw, write or direct an adult. Use one response mode; no separate participation form.

Arrival

BUILD · SCIENCE · W13A · 5 MINUTES

Four clues to start

Choose a route. Four checks help your teacher decide what support is useful today.

Supported · 4 questions

1. Change

Compare A and B. What changes: sample or timer?

Help beside the question
Use the plan card.

Answer guidance

Answer: Sample.

2. Measure

Water collected is recorded in mL or kg?

Help beside the question
Volume uses mL.

Answer guidance

Answer: mL.

3. Same

Both trials use 5 mL input: same or different?

Help beside the question
It is a control.

Answer guidance

Answer: Same.

4. Pilot

Does practice P prove the final A/B result?

Help beside the question
Practice checks method.

Answer guidance

Answer: No.

Standard · 4 questions

1. Question

Name the change and measured result.

Help beside the question
Sample / collected water.

Answer guidance

Answer: Change sample; measure collected water in mL.

2. Control

Name three important controls.

Help beside the question
Use time, input and geometry.

Answer guidance

Answer: For example: 120 seconds, 5 mL input, matched exposed area.

3. Repeat

Why plan repeated valid trials?

Help beside the question
Think consistency and variation.

Answer guidance

Answer: To see variation and whether a pattern repeats.

4. Blank

Why are final result cells empty?

Help beside the question
The comparison has not occurred.

Answer guidance

Answer: No final observations have been collected.

Stretch · 4 questions

1. Geometry

Why can thickness be a confounding variable?

Help beside the question
Water must pass through the specimen.

Answer guidance

Answer: Different thickness gives another possible cause of flow differences.

2. Dry start

Why not silently repeat with the same wet piece?

Help beside the question
The starting condition changes.

Answer guidance

Answer: Its water state differs, so trials are not equivalent.

3. Pilot

Distinguish the pilot question from the science question.

Help beside the question
Method works / samples differ.

Answer guidance

Answer: Pilot checks procedure; final comparison addresses sample through-flow.

4. Feasibility

What if comparable sealed samples cannot be prepared?

Help beside the question
Use honest limits or fixed evidence.

Answer guidance

Answer: Use an approved labelled fixed-data route rather than claim a controlled practical.

Starter

BUILD · SCIENCE · W13A · 4 MINUTES

Too many differences

A gets 5 mL for 120 s; B gets 10 mL for 60 s. Can a difference be attributed to sample alone?

No answer chosen yet. Think or discuss first.

I do

BUILD · SCIENCE · W13A · 7 MINUTES

Make the science visible

Predict, model, explain

Change __. Measure __ in __. Keep __ the same. Pilot __ first.

Choose each view. Describe the evidence before giving a conclusion.

Which supplied sample lets more water reach the collector in 120 seconds under this method?

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

“Change one thing” is a controlled-comparison aim, not a guarantee that natural specimens are identical. Area, thickness, dry state, seals and starting conditions can confound through-flow. A seal leak invalidates the flow inference. Plan repeats with dry matched pieces; repeated wetting of the same piece changes its starting condition. The linked W14 lessons are review/evidence lessons, not a promised full permeability investigation.

Local explainer · 32 seconds · silent with captions

Use instead of part of the demonstration. It never autoplays and needs no internet.

Full text / no-video alternative

00–08 seconds · Ask a clear question
Which supplied sample lets more water reach the collector in 120 seconds under this method?

08–16 seconds · Change and measure
Change the sample. Measure water collected below in mL. Do not confuse a wet top with through-flow.

16–24 seconds · Hold the controls
Use 5 mL input, 120 seconds and matched prepared area and thickness. Control dry start, seal and equipment too.

24–32 seconds · Pilot before final trials
Practise with a separate sample or fictional pilot log. Keep final results blank until an approved comparison occurs.

Planning uses dry cards and diagrams only. Staff decide whether matched, sealed, measurable samples and a safe rig are feasible. No pupil cutting or sample preparation. A future practical needs separate local risk assessment and approval; otherwise use clearly labelled fixed evidence.

Use the evidence together

Use a clue; explain the group

Select a card, then select its group. Keyboard, pointing and paper routes work too. You can move a card when your reasoning changes.

CHANGE

MEASURE

KEEP THE SAME

You may ask for a clearer diagram, fewer cards at once, reading help or more thinking time. Tell your teacher, ask privately, point or pass. Your teacher will say what can change and check whether it helped. No extra sheet is needed.

Show your science

Supported · build your explanation

1. Plan

Select one CHANGE and one MEASURE card.

Help: Sample / water collected in mL.

2. Control

Choose three SAME cards.

Help: 5 mL, 120 s and matched geometry.

3. Prepare

Choose a pilot check and safety stop.

Help: Keep final results blank.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Change sample; measure collected water in mL. Choose relevant controls and a leak/instability stop.

Standard · build your explanation

1. Question

State a sample-comparison question with method and unit.

Help: Use 120 seconds and mL.

2. Method

Name the change, result and at least three justified controls.

Help: Explain how each reduces an alternative cause.

3. Readiness

Plan repeats, a separate pilot and a stop rule.

Help: No final values yet.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

A complete plan includes 5 mL input, 120 s, matching geometry and a separate pilot. Final results stay blank.

Stretch · build your explanation

1. Audit

Identify geometry, dry state and seal risks.

Help: Natural variation remains.

2. Improve

Specify how repeats avoid changing the start condition.

Help: Staff-prepared matched dry pieces or fixed route.

3. Boundary

Explain what the pilot and later review cannot claim.

Help: No unperformed investigation.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

A dry matched-piece plan or labelled fixed route is acceptable. A pilot tests procedure; W14 review does not become a completed A/B experiment.

Repair the proposed plan

Use the digital choices or the matching paper page. One response mode is enough.

Revisit the model

Which supplied sample lets more water reach the collector in 120 seconds under this method?

Refine one explanation

Check that the explanation follows the supplied observation and keeps the stated limit.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

A complete plan includes 5 mL input, 120 s, matching geometry and a separate pilot. Final results stay blank.

Exit

BUILD · SCIENCE · W13A · 2 MINUTES

Two small checks

Supported · 2 questions

1. Change

What changes in the proposed comparison?

Help beside the question
Sample A / B.

Answer guidance

Answer: Sample code.

2. Measure

Collected water is measured in __.

Help beside the question
Volume unit.

Answer guidance

Answer: mL.

Standard · 2 questions

1. Control

Name two controls.

Help beside the question
Read the plan.

Answer guidance

Answer: Any two of input, time, area, thickness, dry start, seal or measuring setup.

2. Pilot

What is the pilot checking?

Help beside the question
Procedure or final winner?

Answer guidance

Answer: The procedure and recording.

Stretch · 2 questions

1. Fairness

Must a fair test give equal results?

Help beside the question
Method fairness is not outcome equality.

Answer guidance

Answer: No.

2. Boundary

Why must final cells remain blank today?

Help beside the question
No final comparison was run.

Answer guidance

Answer: Filling them would invent final evidence.

Knowledge organiser

BUILD Science · W13A · Shared resource

Learning objective

I can plan a controlled water-passage comparison and a separate method pilot.

Key words

variable — A factor that can change.

control — An important factor held consistent.

repeat — Another trial of the same method.

pilot — A small practice run to test the procedure.

Remember

  • Change the sample code; measure water collected below in mL.
  • Keep 5 mL input and 120 seconds consistent.
  • Control area, thickness, dry start, seal and measuring setup.
  • A plan or pilot is not a completed comparison.

Success looks like

  • Name the change and measure with a unit.
  • Specify at least three important controls.
  • Plan repeats, a pilot and a safety stop without inventing results.

Change __. Measure __ in __. Keep __ the same. Pilot __ first.

Word help

variable
A factor that can change.
control
An important factor held consistent.
repeat
Another trial of the same method.
pilot
A small practice run to test the procedure.

TA Brief

Current stage

Current stage:

Preparation and access

Planning uses dry cards and diagrams only. Staff decide whether matched, sealed, measurable samples and a safe rig are feasible. No pupil cutting or sample preparation. A future practical needs separate local risk assessment and approval; otherwise use clearly labelled fixed evidence.

Scientific care

“Change one thing” is a controlled-comparison aim, not a guarantee that natural specimens are identical. Area, thickness, dry state, seals and starting conditions can confound through-flow. A seal leak invalidates the flow inference. Plan repeats with dry matched pieces; repeated wetting of the same piece changes its starting condition. The linked W14 lessons are review/evidence lessons, not a promised full permeability investigation.

Responsive feedback within teaching

The lesson teacher hears an optional request, explains what can change, tries it and checks the effect. Passing or asking privately is valid. No compulsory participation task or new pupil form. Do not infer assessment codes from a click, download or written box.

Sources and scope

  • Original Made by Matt lesson
  • USGS: aquifers, porosity and permeability
  • DfE: science programmes of study

Evidence cards · 1

BUILD Science · W13A · Shared resource

Sample code

Compare Sample A with Sample B in a later approved comparison.

Water collected below / mL

Record the amount reaching the collector after the stated time.

Prepared area and thickness

Dry starting condition

BUILD Science · Sugar Evidence: Read the Label · Supported

Your task

1. Use these fictional teaching cards. All give sugar in g per 100 g: A — 4 g; B — 9 g; C — 14 g; D — 23 g.

Help with this question

Use a paper strip to track one card at a time. Say or point to the letter, the sugar number and ‘g per 100 g’ together.

2. Put the four cards in order from LEAST sugar per 100 g to MOST. Point, move paper cards or direct an adult.

Help with this question

Compare two numbers first. Place the smaller one towards LEAST, then find where each remaining card belongs.

3. Complete: Label ___ has the least sugar per 100 g. Label ___ has the most.

Help with this question

Look at the two ends of your own order. Use those card letters to fill the gaps.

4. Choose the claim we can support: 'A has less sugar per 100 g than D' / 'A is the healthiest food for everyone'.

Help with this question

Ask: does this sentence describe the sugar evidence, or claim to know everything about the food?

5. Finish or point: These sugar numbers show ONE PART OF NUTRITION / THE WHOLE EATING PATTERN. Keep “g per 100 g” with each number.

Help with this question

Look at what was measured. Think about whether these cards show every nutrient and everything a person eats.

BUILD Science · Sugar Evidence: Read the Label · Standard

Your task

1. Read these fictional teaching labels. Each is PER 100 g. A: carbohydrate 22 g; of which sugars 4 g. B: carbohydrate 67 g; of which sugars 9 g. C: carbohydrate 58 g; of which sugars 14 g. D: carbohydrate 72 g; of which sugars 23 g.

Help with this question

Track the ‘of which sugars’ row. Keep the carbohydrate and sugar rows separate.

2. Make a results row for each label. Copy the SUGAR value with its unit and basis; do not copy total carbohydrate.

Help with this question

Use the headings Label | Sugar / g per 100 g. Check each copied value against its nutrient name.

3. Order A–D from least to most sugar per 100 g.

Help with this question

Check adjacent pairs: is each value no larger than the next? Recheck that all four use the same basis.

4. Write or say one comparison: 'Label ___ has ___ g sugar per 100 g. This is less/more than ___.'

Help with this question

Build the comparison from two complete readings. Include which label you are comparing it with.

5. Explain one thing these sugar numbers cannot tell us about the whole food or eating pattern.

Help with this question

Choose one missing piece of information. Explain why that missing information limits a wider judgement.

BUILD Science · Sugar Evidence: Read the Label · Stretch

Your task

1. Fictional labels, all PER 100 g: A — carbohydrate 22 g, sugars 4 g; B — carbohydrate 67 g, sugars 9 g; C — carbohydrate 58 g, sugars 14 g; D — carbohydrate 72 g, sugars 23 g.

Help with this question

Identify the nutrient and reference amount before selecting numerical evidence.

2. Extract the four sugar values and order them. Keep the unit and basis.

Help with this question

Audit the completed order against the source labels; a correct number copied from the wrong row is still the wrong evidence.

3. Extra label E says 'sugars 3 g per 25 g serving'. Someone puts E before A because 3 is less than 4. Audit this decision.

Help with this question

Compare the reference quantities before comparing the two bare numbers.

4. Put E on a per-100 g basis before comparing. How many 25 g servings make 100 g? Then place E among A–D.

Help with this question

Find the scale factor from 25 g of food to 100 g of food. Apply the same factor to the sugar amount.

5. Write one supported comparison from A–D and repair this claim: 'The lowest-sugar card proves the best food for everybody.'

Help with this question

Separate a justified numerical comparison from a wider judgement. State exactly what the evidence establishes and what it leaves unknown.

Answers · Standard

BUILD Science · W13A · Standard

Four-question arrival

1. Question: Change sample; measure collected water in mL.

2. Control: For example: 120 seconds, 5 mL input, matched exposed area.

3. Repeat: To see variation and whether a pattern repeats.

4. Blank: No final observations have been collected.

Two-check exit

1. Control: Any two of input, time, area, thickness, dry start, seal or measuring setup.

2. Pilot: The procedure and recording.
